newsitem.title: USA: Dlr softer at U.S. close, eyes Japanese rate talk.
newsitem.headline: Dlr softer at U.S. close, eyes Japanese rate talk.

text.p: The dollar closed moderately weaker against the yen on Monday after two senior Japanese politicians suggested interest rates in Japan might soon head higher, currency experts said.
The Bank of Japan's (BOJ) official discount rate has been at a record low of 0.5 percent since September 1995.
The remarks fueled demand for yen in Asia, which carried over when trade got underway in Europe and New York.
"They're buying yen and selling everything that's been bought the last couple of weeks," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar closed at 111.09/16 yen and 1.5304/11 marks, down from 111.40/45 yen and 1.5311/14 marks at the open.

Shizuka Kamei, head of the Liberal Democratic Party press office, was quoted in news reports as saying on Monday that a rise in Japan's official discount rate will probably be considered after general elections. Elections are set for October 20.
Separately, Ichiro Ozawa, head of the main opposition New Frontier Party or Shinshinto, also said on Monday that Japan's interest rate levels must be corrected.
The BOJ declined to comment.

Although the politicians' comments jolted a foreign exchange market sensitive to signs that rates in Japan will climb, some analysts dismissed the comments as a ploy to please Japanese savers dissatisfied with the country's rock-bottom interest rates.
"I view it mainly as political posturing ahead of the election," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International.
"I don't think either party is serious about raising rates without economic justification for it," he added.

Growing optimism that the European Union will successfully launch a common currency as planned in January 1999 continued to pressure the mark relative to some other European currencies, currency experts said.
The European Union's monetary committee meets on Tuesday to move forward on key factors including a budget stability pact for countries joining the single currency.

"I think that there's no question the overall consensus of the market is that EMU (European Monetary Union) will go ahead and will go ahead on schedule," said William Marr, manager of foreign exchange at Credit Commerciale De France.
"It's just a question now of a little bit of jockeying in terms of what the market consensus is on who are going to be the first members," Marr said.
The mark traded around 989.75/0.25 Italian lira and 3.3784/87 French francs in late dealings, down from 990.75/1.00 lira and 3.3817/22 francs earlier in the session.
Expectations that Italy will soon re-enter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) also bolstered the lira.
"The market is reluctant to sell off lira with the possibility the French and Germans will insist on lira appreciation before ERM entry," Ruesch's McCarthy said.
The lira crashed out of the ERM during a currency crisis in September 1992.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi requested last week that talks start quickly on the level at which the lira might re-enter the system.
Elsewhere, the dollar closed at 1.2541/46 Swiss francs, off from 1.2562/72 at the open. The dollar ended little changed at Canadian $1.3530/35 compared with C$1.3531/36.
The pound inched up to $1.5633/40 from $1.5628/35 and the Australian dollar rose to $0.7873/78 from $0.7861/66.
-- Donna Sells 212 859 1668
